title: CORS & preflight: the browser's rule, the server's opt-in
objectives: Explain the same-origin policy and what CORS relaxes: the request may still run; CORS decides whether the page can read the response
Predict whether a `fetch` call is preflighted from its method, headers and `Content-Type` (the Fetch standard's safelists)
Write the response headers for a credentialed cross-origin API: the exact origin, `Allow-Credentials: true`, explicit header names, `Vary: Origin`
Explain why curl and server-to-server calls never see CORS, and why CORS is not server-side access control

questions.prompt: Which URL is the **same origin** as `https://app.example.com`?

options.text: `https://app.example.com/settings?tab=2`
`https://api.example.com`
`http://app.example.com`
`https://app.example.com:8443`

questions.explanation: An origin is scheme + host + port; path and query don't count. A different subdomain is a different host, `http` is a different scheme, and `:8443` is a different port from the default `443` — each of those is cross-origin, so a call from the app needs the other origin's CORS permission.

questions.prompt: `curl https://api.partner.test/rates` returns JSON. The same URL from your web app's `fetch` fails with a CORS error. Where is the fix?

options.text: On the server: it must send `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` for your origin — or you call it from your own backend instead
In the page: add `mode: "no-cors"` to the `fetch`
In the page: send `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` as a request header
Force HTTP/1.1; curl works because it doesn't use HTTP/2

questions.explanation: CORS is the *responding* origin granting permission; nothing in the request can grant it. `mode: "no-cors"` makes the request succeed with an opaque response whose body and headers your script can't read — the error goes away and so does the data. curl works because it isn't a browser and doesn't implement CORS at all. If you don't control the API, proxy it through your own server, where CORS doesn't apply.

questions.prompt: A page calls `fetch("https://api.other.test/track?event=click")` — a plain `GET`. The endpoint sends no CORS headers, and the script gets `TypeError: Failed to fetch`. Did the endpoint's handler run?

options.text: Yes — the request was sent and handled; the browser only withheld the response from the script
No — the browser blocked the request before sending it
No — the preflight failed, so the `GET` was never sent
It ran, but the browser replaced the response with a `403`

questions.explanation: A plain `GET` is a simple request: no preflight, sent immediately. The server logged it and ran the handler; then the browser checked the response, found no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` for the page's origin, and gave the script a generic network error. That's why a `GET` that changes state is dangerous whatever your CORS headers say — and why CORS errors don't mean "nothing happened".

questions.prompt: Which cross-origin call goes out **without** a preflight?

options.text: `fetch(url, { method: "POST", body: new URLSearchParams({ q: "tea" }) })`
`fetch(url, { method: "POST", headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }, body })`
`fetch(url, { headers: { Authorization: "Bearer …" } })`
`fetch(url, { method: "PUT", body: "x" })`

questions.explanation: No preflight needs a safelisted method (`GET`, `HEAD`, `POST`) *and* only safelisted headers. `URLSearchParams` sends `application/x-www-form-urlencoded;charset=UTF-8`, which is one of the three safelisted `Content-Type` values — it's what an HTML form could send anyway. `application/json` isn't safelisted, `Authorization` isn't a safelisted header, and `PUT` isn't a safelisted method.

questions.prompt: The API answers `200` with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. The app calls it with `credentials: "include"`. What does the app's script get?

options.text: A `TypeError` — with credentials, `*` doesn't count, so the browser won't share the response
The JSON — `Allow-Credentials: true` makes the wildcard acceptable
The JSON, but the cookies weren't sent
The JSON — the browser treats `*` as the page's origin

questions.explanation: The Fetch standard's table: credentials mode `include` + `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` is not shared, whatever `Allow-Credentials` says. The request *was* sent with cookies and the server *did* answer `200` — the browser just won't hand it to the script. The fix is to echo the exact origin. (Tested in Chrome: `TypeError: Failed to fetch`.)

questions.prompt: Two front-ends, `https://app.example.com` and `https://admin.example.com`, call the same API with cookies. How does the API allow both?

options.text: Compare the request's `Origin` with a list of both, echo the matching one, and send `Vary: Origin`
`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com, https://admin.example.com`
`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`
Send two `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` headers, one per origin

questions.explanation: The header holds exactly one origin or `*`, and two copies combine into the same comma-separated list — which matches no origin. With credentials `*` is refused. So the server picks the one origin that matches the request, and because the response now depends on `Origin`, adds `Vary: Origin` so a cache can't serve app's response to admin (or a response with no CORS headers to either).

questions.prompt: "The admin API is safe: its CORS allow-list only contains `https://admin.example.com`." What's wrong with that?

options.text: CORS only controls which *browser pages* may read responses; curl or a script can call the API with any `Origin`, so it still needs real authentication and authorization
Nothing — requests from other origins are rejected
It should use `*` so the allow-list can't be bypassed
It also needs `Access-Control-Max-Age` to be safe

questions.explanation: Outside a browser nothing enforces CORS, and `Origin` is just a header anyone can set: `curl -H 'Origin: https://admin.example.com' …` works. Even in a browser, simple requests reach the server before CORS is consulted. CORS protects users' browsers from other sites reading responses *as them*; every request still needs credentials checked on the server.

prompts.prompt: The browser asks permission before a `PUT` with JSON and a bearer token.
prompts.explanation: A preflight is an `OPTIONS` request carrying the method the real request will use and the names of its non-safelisted headers (lowercased, sorted, comma-separated). It never carries cookies.

prompts.prompt: Grant the app's credentialed request, and keep caches honest.
prompts.explanation: The exact origin (no trailing slash, never `*` with credentials), `true` in lowercase — the Fetch standard compares it case-sensitively — and `Vary: Origin` because the answer depends on which origin asked.

prompts.prompt: Make a cross-origin `fetch` send the user's cookies.
prompts.explanation: `fetch` defaults to `credentials: "same-origin"`, so a cross-origin call carries no cookies unless you ask. With `"include"`, the response is only readable if the server echoes your origin and sends `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`.

prompts.prompt: Let browsers reuse this preflight's answer for ten minutes instead of the default five seconds.
prompts.explanation: `Access-Control-Max-Age` is in seconds; the Fetch standard's default is 5. Browsers cap it — MDN lists 24 hours for Firefox and 2 hours for Chromium (since v76).

code: // Page on http://localhost:4124, API on http://localhost:4123
snippets.question: How many HTTP requests reach the API?
snippets.explanation: No `Content-Type` was set, so `fetch` sends the string as `text/plain;charset=UTF-8` — a safelisted value. `POST` is a safelisted method, so the browser sends it straight away. Add `"Content-Type": "application/json"` and Chrome sends two: an `OPTIONS` preflight, then the `POST`. (Both observed in the API's request log.)

code: // The API answers every request with:
snippets.question: What does the page see?
snippets.answer: Nothing is logged — fetch rejects with TypeError: Failed to fetch
snippets.explanation: The server logged the `GET` and answered `200`, but with credentials included, `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` doesn't count. The browser withholds the whole response, so `fetch` rejects before there's a `res` to log. The script can't even learn the status — the details are only in the browser console.

snippets.question: Does the `PATCH` reach the API?
snippets.answer: No — only the OPTIONS preflight arrives; fetch rejects with TypeError
snippets.explanation: `PATCH` isn't safelisted, so the browser preflights it. The `204` grants the origin but its `Allow-Methods` doesn't include `PATCH`, so the preflight fails and the real request is never sent — the API's log shows the `OPTIONS` and nothing after it. Unlike the simple `GET` earlier, a failed preflight really does stop the request.
